questions.q: What is the difference between the target question and the heuristic question?
options: The target question is the assessment you intend to produce; the heuristic question is the simpler question you answer instead.
The target question is answered by System 2 and the heuristic question by System 1, and both are answered every time.
The heuristic question is the hard one the experimenter asks; the target question is the one the participant invents.
The target question is always about probability; the heuristic question is always about feelings.
questions.explain: Substitution: “If a satisfactory answer to a hard question is not found quickly, System 1 will find a related question that is easier and will answer it.”

questions.q: What is the conjunction fallacy, and why does the Linda problem demonstrate it?
questions.a: Judging a conjunction of two events as more probable than one of them in a direct comparison. Linda fits “feminist” better, so “feminist bank teller” was ranked more likely than “bank teller”, though every feminist bank teller is a bank teller: “When you specify a possible event in greater detail you can only lower its probability.” The problem sets representativeness against logic, and the error stays attractive even when recognised.

questions.q: True or false: When German students were asked how happy they were first, and how many dates they had last month second, the two answers were highly correlated.
questions.explain: The correlation was about zero in that order. It was “about as high as correlations between psychological measures can get” only when the dating question came first, because the emotion it aroused was still present and System 1 had a ready answer.

questions.q: Which of these does the author list among the characteristics of System 1?
options: Weighs the evidence it does not have as carefully as the evidence it has
questions.explain: System 1 focuses on existing evidence and ignores absent evidence (WYSIATI), and it represents sets by norms and prototypes, not by integrating them. The other three are on the author’s closing list.

questions.section: Less is More, Sometimes Even in Joint Evaluation
questions.q: Probability, like economic value, is a sum-like variable, but the author says “System 1 averages instead of ____.”
questions.explain: This is why Hsee’s larger dinnerware set was valued less in single evaluation, and why Linda’s “feminist bank teller” felt more probable.

questions.q: Put the sections of Chapter 9 in the order the author presents them.
questions.explain: The chapter defines substitution first, then shows it at three levels: perception (the 3-D heuristic), self-assessment (the mood heuristic for happiness), and belief (the affect heuristic).

questions.q: Match each term from Chapter 9 to its meaning.
pairs: System 1 finds and answers an easier, related question when a hard one has no quick answer
The assessment you intend to produce
The simpler question you answer instead
Fitting the answer to the original question, such as turning the strength of a feeling into a dollar amount
questions.explain: “If a satisfactory answer to a hard question is not found quickly, System 1 will find a related question that is easier and will answer it.”

questions.q: Which self does each measure speak to?

items.t: “All things considered, how satisfied are you with your life as a whole these days?”

questions.explain: Almost all earlier knowledge of well-being came from a question addressed to the remembering self. The author turned to measuring the experiencing self directly, and the chapter concludes the two are “something else entirely.”

questions.q: What did the Gallup-Healthways data show about income and well-being?
options: Experienced well-being and life satisfaction both rise steadily with income.
Neither experienced well-being nor life satisfaction is related to income.
Experienced well-being keeps rising with income, while life satisfaction levels off.
Experienced well-being stops increasing at about $75,000 household income in high-cost areas, while life satisfaction keeps rising.
questions.explain: Poverty makes one miserable; riches may enhance life satisfaction but do not (on average) improve experienced well-being. Life evaluation and actual experience “are also different.”

questions.q: True or false: “Mark has blond hair” versus “Mark has hair” produces the same conjunction fallacy as Linda.
questions.explain: It causes no fallacy, because the added detail is not more plausible. “In the absence of a competing intuition, logic prevails.”
